utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Case No. IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Keegan, are you going to take this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Before we proceed, if may I address the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I have received earlier most of the -- 1200 pages of the exhibits. And we have objected to most of them as you heard yesterday. However, coming to Chicago this time, I have not brought with me those that we have objected and so I didn't have those copies with me. What I have received, a list of the exhibits that are going to be introduced through this witness. Previously to yesterday afternoon, I have only got a notice that one exhibit shall be admitted. And now it seems the long list of them is going to be. So I didn't have them in my possession and I might ask permission of the Court to read them before I would. Because some of them most likely I never read. And some of them, if I did, I will so inform you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, let the witness be sworn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mevludin Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I may begin, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Will you please state for the Trial Chamber your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Mevludin Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in the Municipality of Vlasenica in the Village of Cerska. Since 1964 I have lived in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you please briefly describe for the Trial Chamber your education, background and military service record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary education in Kozarac and I went to grammar school in Prijedor. I started mining and geology at the university in Tuzla. I did my military service with the JNA in 1982, in Leskovac in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what was your military speciality during your service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My military speciality was artillery. I served on Howitzer, 105 millimetres. It was an assignment I could not choose, it was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is your nationality, your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak and a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, do you now hold a political office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a member of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did you join the Party of Democratic Action or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the SDA in June, 1990. It was immediately after it was established in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was also involved in the creation of the party branch in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you please briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what caused the development of political parties in the Former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Political parties in the Former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were created in the period which was characterised by a series of reforms, which took place in the South Eastern Europe. And Yugoslavia also experienced the same fate. The former republics of Slovenia and Croatia were the first republics to join such a process. People remember very well the situation at that time. There was a -- it was a period of democratic awakening and the objective was to topple the communist governments. In a number of countries, this process took place peacefully and democratic changes took place. In former Yugoslav republics, population felt, people realised that it was a chance for them to become democratic and a series of movements took place. There was a series of changes in law which enabled the creation of democratic parties in the area. We joined that process and we decided to establish the Party of Democratic Action in Prijedor and to join this process of transformation and change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you please describe, what were the other main parties that developed in Bosnia and Herzegovina at this time and in Prijedor municipality as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is important to note that until that time, there was only one party that had the power, the League of Communists. There was a number of organisations, but they were under the control of the communist party and they were not real political parties. The party that had power at that time and the segment of the society which enjoyed the support of the party in power, did not like the idea of having new parties. And several parties were developed from the former communist party and it was the so-called left bloc. All others who did not take part in the power in the old system, established other parties, created other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. You're talking about very complicated and difficult issues, could you slow down just a bit for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do that. Thank you. Except for the former communists, whose party was transformed into the SDP party, and Democratic Socialist Union, and Socialist Social Reformers and to the Liberal party, the Party of Democratic Action was established, the Croatian Democratic Party, a Serb Democratic Party, Serb Radical Party and Croatian Democratic Union. At the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a number of other parties, but I will confine myself to the area of Prijedor. And these parties were established in Prijedor, the parties that I have just enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you please describe the general identification of each of the parties, that is, what ethnic group, if any, were they associated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only partly the case. First of all, there was the Serb Radical Party, which was established and was identified with the Serb Radical Party, which had been established prior to that in Serbia. Its leader was Vojislav Seselj. He was very well known in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia and in the international community in general because of his radical convictions and radical actions and other things that he did later on, which were basically violations of the international humanitarian law. The leader of the radical party in Prijedor was a Mr. Stojan Vracar who was from Omarska. He was a teacher as far as I can remember. In addition to the Serb Radical Party, as a party identified with the Serb people, the Serb Democratic Party was established as well. Bosniaks, Muslims were members, most of them, of the Party of Democratic Action or the SDA. According to its programme, it was not an exclusively national party. However, due to the circumstances in which it functioned, the process -- and because the process of the homogenisation of the Serb people was already completed because of the influences coming from the neighbouring Republic of Serbia and because of the same process that happened with the Croatian segment of the population, because of the influence of the neighbouring Republic of Croatia and its official policy, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian people decided to establish the Croatian Democratic Union, which was a branch of the Croatian Democratic Union in Croatia. So, in view of the circumstances, the Party of Democratic Action was formerly a party of the Bosniak Muslim segment of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, thanks to our programme, and thanks to our efforts, we managed to win over a certain number of members, a certain percentage of members and even officials coming from other national communities in the republic. Of course, in the period that followed, it was treated as a party of Bosniaks and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You discussed briefly the Serb Radical Party and you mentioned its -- the leader of the party, Vojislav Seselj, did he ever, in fact, visit the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember for sure that he visited Prijedor on two occasions. There was rumours that he came to Prijedor on more than two occasions, but I can only vouch for two such occasions. His first visit was in the area of Omarska or Maricka. This was related to me by a number of my colleagues. We used to live in that area. This took place in a very -- during a very tense period, but during the period through which people still communicated with each other. The second occasion was prior to the war in Prijedor and, according to the information I received, he was in the Prijedor town itself. According to some sources, he was accommodated in the local hotel in Prijedor, but I cannot be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there any physical evidence that you, yourself, saw in the municipality that there were followers of the Serbian Radical Party in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course it was obvious and one could see, one could realise that such a party existed. I have to draw your attention to an important fact in my opinion. A long time before the elections, some 10 months before the elections took place and before all these changes took place, one could see a number of graffiti celebrating Seselj in the area. The graffiti, which were actually some Chetnik signs, signs that belonged to the criminal Chetnik formations during the Second World War. These people were celebrated and revered as heroes by the members of the radical party. One could see graffiti that were also very common at that time in Serbia, all Serbs should live in one state. I can give you a few examples. You could see such graffiti on the way from Prijedor to Banja Luka on the railway line. At the railway station in Omarska, before you enter the railway station, on the left hand side on one of the administration buildings of the railway station, there was a graffiti that says, "Long Live Seselj". And, also, "This is in Serbia." This took place before the new parties were created. There was also writing that said Serb Chetnik movement. We could also see a number of signs, such as "for us," signs that later became official with the Serb people. Of course all this had a very negative influence on the population in Prijedor and all attempts to identify perpetrators, people who were writing these slogans, were to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was it about the programme or policies of the Serb Radical Party that from this kind of graffiti would cause a negative influence on the population in Prijedor, what was the concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to underline that the Serb Radical Party always had very clear positions. Let me give you several postulates of the programme of this party. All Serbs in one state. It's a very transparent and a very clear objective and it was part of the programme of that party. Second, they claimed and they insisted on it, that wherever there is a single Serb grave, that that was Serb land. And they even went so far as to propound some morbid thesis. They abused certain tragedies that befell the Serb people during the Second World War. They kept saying that Jasenovac was the largest Serb town, largest that was underground. This had terrible consequences on one hand on the Serb people, which experienced some kind of nationalistic awakening at the time. On the other hand, it instilled terror among other segments of the population. Also, there was the idea that the Serb land was bordered by Serb graves. And then there was also the idea that wherever there was a Serb grave for Serbs, that that was the Serb land. And according on the basis of these ideas, you could see a number of graffiti in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The most common was one, this is Serbia. This was one of their main ideas. I could give you a number of that, but these were the most common ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Well the concept as a general principle that the Serbs would want to live in an unified state, in and of itself is not a problematic concept. The question is, why did it instil terror in the non-Serbs? What was it about this position of the Serb Radical Party that caused fear in non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fear was caused by the fact that they were proclaiming Serb lands, also lands where non-Serbs were living. While not recognising their identity on nationality, they said that Muslims don't exist. It's a conjured up nationality. These are people who betrayed their faith. They should be -- they even went so far at some rallies, they stated these are people which should be killed, who should be evicted. We knew that they were the followers of the Chetnik movement from the Second World War. We knew that because their ideas in their political programs were the ideas of Stevan Moljevic who from the Second World War and who had a very decisive plan concerning Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had a project. He drew a project where a certain percentage would be Christian, one would be evicted, expelled and a percentage killed. These are facts which can be also confirmed in the archives, in Serbia this is the Moljevic programme, later the Nedic programme we were afraid of the fact that the Serb--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am just going to interrupt you for a moment. Mr. Keegan, yesterday we intervened during the cross-examination of witnesses saying that these events which were being talked of were 50 years ago. Now, if that rule applies to the Defence, it certainly applies to the Prosecution. So, would you confine yourself to relevant matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These issues, and I am attempting to do it briefly. I am hesitant to break in on the witness and interrupt their statements. But the issue this goes to show the state of mind of the individuals during 1990 to 1992. But I will keep it brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I appreciate that. It seems to me you're perfectly entitled to break in on the witness, if you want to do so. I am sure it won't be regarded as discourteous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object the this logic that a Prosecutor is propounding. I mean if he had an expert witness, he could testify as to the state of mind of individuals. This is an occurrence witness, he can testify of what he saw and what he heard. But as to the state of mind, I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can testify to his own state of mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, did you take part in the pre-election campaign in Opstina Prijedor, the Municipality of Prijedor in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At that time, was there cooperation in the Prijedor area between the parties that you have named earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And from your perspective and knowledge of the campaigning process, what was the main focus of developing, or intention of developing, the cooperation between the parties in Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our main objective and the main objective of the party, which I participated in the foundation of, that is the Party of Democratic Action, that was to win over communism and to set up a democratic society, a multi party society, where we wished and made the endeavours in the electoral campaign to establish cooperation on the basis of these principles with all the parties whose goal was, objective was, democratic change. We totally excluded any type of cooperation with the Serb Radical Party. In view of the facts which I have mentioned previously, we wanted to achieve cooperation with the Serb Democratic Party and with the Croatian democratic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And did you have, in fact, some events, or did you take part in some events aimed at developing that cooperation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. In the stage when we had the foundation committees for SDS and SDA, we had cooperation. We had the guarantee of the Serb Democratic Party that they do not support the radical party. And just as the Party of Democratic Action, they wished to have a victory and to defeat the communist. So, in our meetings we also proposed to express this cooperation publicly. We proposed a number of forms. Our first proposal was, when holding electoral rallies that we present ourselves jointly. That the SDA representatives attend the meetings of the SDS and vice versa, that they attend our rallies. And later on, in the pre-electoral stage, we also proposed to print joint propaganda material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you attend any joint rallies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have attended one of the rallies of the Serb Democratic Party, rallies in Cirkin Polje that was in all across the railroad station and it was near the silo. That was a local pre-electoral rally. I also took the floor as a representative of SDA. And there wasn't much difference in my utterances and those of the gentleman from the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And after that rally in Cirkin Polje, did you have the opportunity to attend any other joint rallies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was -- I am speaking of the period now, the president of the two main officials in the foundation committee of the Serb Democratic Party were Mr. Milakovic and Mr. Mirko Curcija. They were recalled from these functions and they weren't any more important figures in the Serb Democratic Party. They were quite open for cooperation, but later on as I said regrettably they were recalled. After that, Mr. Milakovic in the Kozarski Vjesnik, he gave -- granted an interview and he stated that there was an eruption of unimaginable nationalism and that that was the cause that he was recalled because he didn't want to accept this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After that time, did the SDS agree to any more joint rallies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no rallies, no. But we had already achieved an agreement to print a poster jointly, a pre-electoral poster, and despite the recalling of these two people, we insisted that this be completed, that this job be completed, which it also was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Upon consultation with co-counsel, we observe that a previous question had contained some remarks in the newspapers or coming from the third person, what Mr. Milakovic had said after he had resigned, and this does not indicate whether the witness has heard it, seen it, read it, word-read it. If the Prosecutor would like to connect it up, that is absolutely proper, but if there is not any connection, we move that to be stricken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will produce the newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Semenovic, during this period, did you have any contact with the accused, Milan Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the period before we agreed on a joint poster, no, I've never met the gentleman. I saw Mr. Kovacevic for the first time when we were discussing the graphic design of the poster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you became introduced to him and came to know him, what was your knowledge of his position or role in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until then, I knew nothing about his position and his function in the SDS. The first time I met him during these talks on the printing of this joint poster and how we shall present ourselves at the elections. The two parties agreed on such a poster, and our common attitude was to present an idea of the graphic design at this joint meeting with the SDS. The SDA had to give the authority to two members, and the other party also authority to two members, to decide on the graphic design. The Serb Democratic Party proposed that we meet in the new hotel in Prijedor on the first floor in one of the rooms on the upper floors. We, at the time, agreed upon -- we attended the meeting, myself and Mr. Aladin Sijercic from the SDA. Later on, he was killed. He's not alive any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And who was the representative from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we move the non-responsive remarks be stricken or be fully explained as to the extent of knowledge referring to "the gentleman that went to our negotiations, he's no longer alive."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, for the moment, I don't think it's very important whether he is or not from the point of view of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, who was the representative from the SDS for the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came to that meeting and, in the room, we saw twelve people, twelve members of the Serb Democratic Party. This was a bit of a surprise for us because it was decided that there would be two and two, but they explained that they had a previous meeting and that they would all be attending this joint meeting, and we had nothing against that. It was the first time that I met on that occasion Mr. Kovacevic, Dr. Kovacevic, and four of the five who were discussing the possible graphic outlay of the poster. Dr. Kovacevic spoke the longest. His comments and his observations concerned the colours on the poster, then the title, "SDS," where it should be on the poster; on the alphabet, the lettering. They wanted also that the name "Yugoslavia" be present on the poster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Subsequent to this meeting, did you reach an agreement on the poster?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After a few hours of discussions, the gentleman from the SDS asked us to leave the room for some ten minutes so that they could have their own internal consultations. After that, we returned to the room, and they told us that they accept the compromise solution that we submitted. After that, they regularly paid half the price for this poster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there was discussions about the colours on the poster and the alphabet. What were the positions of the SDS and what was the compromise which was reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SDS asked us to remove the name "Bosnia" and "Herzegovina," and to have it "Yugoslavia," namely, and that a part of these posters be printed exclusively in the Cyrillic script and half in the Latin alphabet. They wanted the colours of the existing flag, Yugoslav flag, and I think the flag was -- the colours of the flag were at the bottom of the poster. Then they also demanded that the graphic solution contain the overlapping initials of the two parties, that SDS is not placed vertically but horizontally because SDS, as was proposed, was hanging, and wherever it was possible, we accepted a compromise, and we said, "Okay, we'll place 'Yugoslavia,' but we will not -- we cannot delete 'Bosnia' and 'Herzegovina'." Then we also added we want the simultaneous use of Cyrillic script and the alphabet, Latin alphabet; and after some consultations, this was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After these meetings and as you continued in the political process in Prijedor, did you come to be aware of Dr. Kovacevic's positions in the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got to know about his position later on. For some time, I didn't know, but only later, when it was officially published, his position was officially published, I knew that he was the vice-president of the executive committee of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I could have this exhibit tendered, please? This is Exhibit 7.1 on the Prosecution index of documents submitted earlier. Here are the copies for everyone else, to the Defence, to the witness, and to the Judges. This is not one of the documents that we reached agreement on as of yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, I would direct your attention to the third page of that document, the Kozarski Vjesnik article, entitled "Leaders Dismissed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course I recognise it. This is the article in the local paper which published the piece of news about the dismissal of the leaders, of Mr. Milakovic, Mr. Curcija and some others, and the new leadership was elected, Dr. Srdja Srdic was elected to the presidency, Ranko Gnjatovic as the head of the main board, and as vice-president, Dr. Brane Koncar, Dr. Milan Kovacevic, Professor Milan Pilipovic, Dusan Kurnoga, Nedeljko Katana, and Momcilo Radakovic. So this happened in the beginning -- or at the end of the month of October, beginning of November, and these dismissals had a direct impact on the cooperation between the two parties, SDA and SDS. Here also, in the lower left angle, corner --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Before we proceed, I have to interrupt here because as I informed the Court earlier, that I have not read these documents before, and we objected to the overwhelming majority of documents that were produced, and most of those objections were as to the foundation of the papers, and when I looked at the exhibit, original newspaper clipping, Kozarski Vjesnik, November 2nd, year 19 -- and we don't know what year it was, and if it is not -- and the translation reads 2nd of November, 1990. I move that this exhibit be stricken at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The second page of that document has the cover page of the edition, Your Honour. These were provided to the Defence with the dates available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about whether the accused was the vice-president or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Based on my present knowledge and level of investigation, I cannot ascertain whether he was ever vice-president, and that's why I will take this as indication of such effect if I had -- and I am not nit-picking here, believe me, Your Honour -- if this is translation and translation is on the page and the article, we can't accept this front page. It could be a simple mistake. Because if we are pursuing the truth, we have to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, have we the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We have, Your Honour. And, of course, the offer to view all the originals of all the documents was made back in April -- actually, prior, February it was made, and the offer still stands at any time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could produce the original, and that will resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit this exhibit, but we will call for the production of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, were you also made aware that Dr. Kovacevic was a founding member of his party as you had been a founding member of your party in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection. That is a question that misstates and mischaracterises previous testimony. The witness has testified only that he has seen Dr. Kovacevic when they were -- and he doesn't know anything about his activity in the party until the present exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a leading question anyway. Mr. Keegan, could you rephrase that in a non-leading form, ask the witness what he knows about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- if he knows anything or what the basis of his knowledge is about the accused's role in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, were you made aware of what, if any, role the accused had in the origins of the SDS party in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he had a role in the origins of the SDS party. I wish to repeat, I wish to state to the Court, the SDS delegated a certain number of people to discuss the graphic design of our pre-electoral poster, so this was for the purpose of the pre-electoral poster. All members of -- all the then members of the SDS were founding members, they belonged to the founding segment of the party, all these people, just as all the people who were present there as members of the SDA were also founding members of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I move the response be stricken as conclusory without any basis in fact. We are only -- the witness is surmising of seeing Dr. Kovacevic in a meeting where it's being discussed about a poster, a poster, and that he is the founding member of SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can give the evidence and you can cross-examine about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a question of what weight it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would now tender the document that has been marked on the exhibit of documents number 7.16. Again, this is one that the Defence and the Prosecution have not yet had an opportunity to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the document belonging to the Serb Democratic Party in Prijedor. It was published on the 5th of May, '94. It's a typical party document issued by the personnel committee, and this kind of document concerns a number of prominent members and this is a list of candidates. The first candidate here proposed was Mr. Milan Kovacevic and you have a list of qualifications and the reason why he's being proposed to the office of director. Among other things, it stated that he was an anaesthesiologist and also that he was one of the founding members of the SDS in the area of Prijedor. The document was signed by the president of the municipal board of the SDS, Mr. Ranko Gnjatovic, and it is stamped with a rubber stamp of the Serb Democratic Party. So this is quite clear. It's stated clearly that he was one of the founding members of the party. In addition to Dr. Kovacevic, we have a number of other persons as candidates for various offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Semenovic, just referring back to the Kozarski Vjesnik article that we had looked at. It had described there the election for the main board, the municipal board, of the SDS in Prijedor. Can you please describe what the role and purpose of a main board for the political party is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role of such a board within a political party is to elect or to appoint officials of the party, to confirm their office or to replace them from function. That is the highest party body at the level of the municipality. Such a body would elect the president of the party, that is, they would propose a candidate who would then have to be approved by the central board in Sarajevo. They proposed officials for various offices at the level of the municipality. It drafts the policy of the party at the local level. Local officials are accountable to the main board for the implementation of the policy of the party or for failure to implement such policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in that Exhibit 7.1, is there, in fact, a --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to object to what has happened here. I think this is inadvertent and for whatever reason it happened because the question was: What were the functions of the president of the executive committee --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Of the executive committee on the municipality level, and the witness is testifying as to what would be the functions of the party executive board president, and I think if he can just clarify this so that we are not confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, that actually wasn't the question. I believe the question was: What was the role and function of the municipal board of the party in the municipality? And that was what the answer was, Your Honour. It was the board itself I was after, not the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Also, Mr. Semenovic, on that Exhibit 7.1, is there also a depiction of the poster which you have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but I have to emphasise that you can only see one part of the text, and in its integrity, the text was the following: "We, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, have always been and shall remain together." And according to the compromise that was reached with members of the SDS, we added also "in Yugoslavia." You can see it on the right side of the poster. And the text was therefore, "In our Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, we shall be and we shall remain always together." In the middle of the poster, there was a geographical map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and inside the borders, there were two abbreviations, two initials of the two parties overlapping, so that they're connected with one letter that they have in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Semenovic, what were the results of the elections held in November of 1990 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the election results, the Party of Democratic Action won, second came the Serb Democratic Party, and the remaining votes went to the opposition parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the margin of victory? What was the difference in the results between the SDA and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the results, out of the total of 90 seats, the SDA won 30 seats, the Serb Democratic Party won 28 seats, and the remaining seats went to other opposition parties. The difference, that is the margin of victory, the results as represented in percentage, were 44 per cent SDA and forty-two point something for SDS, but you can see it for the number of seats at the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, as a general matter, what would that result mean with respect to the appointment of positions in the municipal administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This result meant that the Party of Democratic Action had the right to appoint its candidate to the highest level office within the municipality; that is, the office of the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the SDS contest the results of the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially, at various press conferences, the SDS claimed that the elections were somehow rigged, they tried to contest the results of the elections, but they had no evidence for that, so finally, the results were accepted by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We seem to have lost our usher. Thank you, Mr. Bos. If I may continue as regard to the second round of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, I would direct your attention to the article entitled, "National Composition Causes Dissatisfaction." Do you recognise that article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, but I, maybe I have the wrong document, because I cannot find the title you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see it either. It seems that a translation has been an attached to the different original that does not comport to translation, a mix up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Keegan, perhaps you might review that during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hand that back for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I refer to the document that I have in front of me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, not for the moment. Later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would now tender the document marked 5.2 on the index. That first one was 5.1, Your Honour. Mr. Semenovic, in that document I refer you to, I believe it's the fourth page, the article entitled, "Compromise on New Elections."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have found the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would refer you specifically to the comments of Srdja Srdic as are represented in that article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Srdic claims here that the agreement could not be reached within the expected period and he says that he doesn't believe that the agreement would be reached, the agreement concerning that division of power. And, therefore, it would be necessary to have the old authorities in place for additional period of one month. Within this period, no agreement is reached. He believes that new elections should be organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We would offer that, Your Honour. This was one of the documents agreed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, you indicated earlier that the challenge to the legality of the elections did not succeed. Thereafter, how did the process of the formation of the new government proceed in the Opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The process of the formation of the new government was very difficult. We can divide it into two stages. The first stage that followed immediately the elections, which was the stage of the appointment of main officials within the municipality, that first stage was without problems. However, when we reached the phase of appointed president of the executive committee, president of the municipality and so on, this was a very difficult period. And we experienced a number of obstacles throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And are those difficulties what Dr. Srdic referring to in the article, the exhibit we just viewed, 5.2?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to this line of questioning and these type of answers. Because Mr. Semenovic was elected on the same elections and one of the exhibit standard explains as a member of the parliament of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So unless he indicates where he participated in those negotiations or somehow has been consulted, it would be proper, but otherwise by his function heretofore presented, it seems he wouldn't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you can establish the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I was, in attempt to speed things up, as requested by the trial, I was leaving out some of the foundation material which is clearly stated in the prior testimony of this witness which the Defence had. But I will go back to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, as Mr. Vucecevic just indicated, you were elected to a position in the November elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was elected to Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Chamber of Mmunicipalities. I was elected in the second round of elections because in the first round none of the candidates garnered a sufficient amount of votes. And in the second round, the number of candidates was reduced to two and the one who gained the majority of votes was then elected to the republican parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the Chamber of Municipalities, that is one of two chambers in the republican parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And that was one of the two chambers, the Chamber of Citizens and the Chamber of Municipalities. The Chamber of Municipalities was composed of representatives; namely, from each municipality, one such representative was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During this initial phase after the November elections, did you participate in the formation of the government in the Opstina of Prijedor, as well as attending duties at the Republican Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. The level of municipal level and the level of the Republic, these are two different notions, two different levels. As a member of the republican parliament, my only link with the municipality was in the sense that certain problems, which I observe in the municipality, I could raise them and try to resolve them on the republican level, in the republican parliament. And, according to my function, I had no right to participate in the formation of the municipal authority, government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Keegan, I wonder if we may move on from here. The minutiae of the formation of this government, I don't think is going to assist us very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact is the problem of the political process, which later on is responsible for the take-over by force. So we do think that there is some need to at least cover the fact that the political democratic process did not proceed smoothly and what were the problems. And there will be a demonstrable link to the events that then occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that things have not proceeded smoothly and you've produced some documents in relation to that. Perhaps we can now move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With respect to the agreement that was eventually reached on distribution of power, did that -- was that agreement, in fact, reached at the republic level and then transmitted down to the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This is Document 6.1 on the exhibit list, Your Honour. And it is one of the documents agreed to by the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, we admit it. It will admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it. This is the document which has been coordinated on the level of the leaderships of the three national parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And after this coordination, all the parties informed the municipal boards concerning these criteria for the distribution of municipal functions and departments. The criteria here are specified quite clearly. They're expressed in percentages and on the level of municipalities, what remained to be done was to apply these criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Semenovic, I would note that in this document there are two different documents, one which is dated 22 December, 1990 and one which is not dated. Can you indicate for the Court which of these documents came first, which of these agreements came first and which was second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first agreement which had been achieved -- just a moment please. The first one was achieved on the 22nd of December. After that, criteria were defined immediately after, two or three days later, these criteria were defined as you see them here without a date. I had partial view and insight in this coordination because in connection with this, I stayed in Sarajevo a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And, sir, when you were not in Sarajevo, you were back in the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the Municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And during that time you were back at home, would you continue in your role as a member of the SDA, participating in the municipal political issues as a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as a member, and as a Vice-President of the party. Because after the election into the party, I was also elected to the post of Vice-President of the SDA party for Municipality of Prijedor and, in this capacity, I was then involved in some of these political issues and business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, based on this agreement that was reached at the republic level, it would appear then that under the agreement, in fact, the SDA was entitled to pick first in the choice of positions in the municipality, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How were the candidates for the municipal positions nominated and elected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The candidates were nominated by the parties and they were elected by the Municipal Assembly. In line with the inter party agreement, which had already been achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now which position did the SDA select as its first choice in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had the right, on the basis of the electoral results, to cover the first and foremost post in the municipality, the President of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What position did the SDS then select as its first choice in the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said the SDA has opted for the position of the president of the municipal assembly and, according to the agreement, the next one was SDS and they chose the function for the highest function, the President of the Executive Board of the Assembly, of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And who was their candidate for that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their candidate was Dr. Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was his candidacy then confirmed by the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the municipal assembly confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We would now offer another Kozarski Vjesnik article, Your Honour, it's Document No. 7.2 on the list. This is not one of the ones which the parties have had the opportunity to discuss yet. Mr. Semenovic, do you recognise that article?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could you give us some latitude here, so we can read this document? I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let the witness go through and refer to the points that he wants to. Then, if necessary, you can have a moment during the adjournment to have a look at anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what does this article reflect, Mr. Semenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This article is a journalist report from the constituent meeting of the Municipal Assembly where the new leadership was appointed on the basis of the results. You can see also an insert here, on the right hand side where you have the photographs of the two leading municipal officials, Professor Cehajic, and Dr. Milan Kovacevic. And under the photographs there are short biographies of the short curricula of the two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And in the article it reflects the election of the municipal officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and the curricular of the two new officers are also presented in the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just a moment please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It describes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It states that after the elections and the appointment of the two officials, that they solemnly were taking the oath that they were then also congratulated by Mr. Milakovic, the former president, and then they have taken over solemnly their new functions. And then they both addressed the Assembly with short welcoming addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Does the article also indicate who were elected to the deputy positions for those two jobs, that is the Deputy President of the Municipal Assembly, and the Deputy President of the Executive Committee of the Assembly? Who was elected as the Deputy of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it stands that it was Mr. Milomir Stakic and the Deputy President of the Executive Committee Enes Kursumovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I believe the witness actually said Dr. Milomir Stakic, was Milomir Stakic a doctor, Mr. Semenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, if I recollect, if my recollection serves me, but I would like to check it in the text, but I can't read it. It's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll move on. What position would Milomir Stakic later hold after the take-over of power in April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on he occupied the post as the head of the crisis staff, and the President of the Serb Assembly of Prijedor, but that was at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what party was Milomir Stakic affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member of the SDS. And, in fact, he was a member of the leadership of SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And, sir, if you know, what later happened to Mohamed Cehajic, the President of the Municipal Assembly, after the take-over of power in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After power was taken over in April, 1992, Mohamed Cehajic, and all the other non-Serbs were banned, had no band to their offices and there they had no access to the premises where they carried out their functions. And twenty days after the coup, they were all arrested and a greater number of these people were regrettably killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are matters which the witness could only speak of second-hand and we should have first-hand evidence, if possible on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Go on until five past eleven, if you would, Mr. Keegan, we started late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To make clear then your knowledge of these events, Mr. Semenovic, did you personally know Mohamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him very well. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Since the end of the hostilities in 1995, after the Dayton accords, have you travelled throughout Bosnia and been a participant in the SDA party once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In part, yes. But there were certain areas where I couldn't go in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And in any of the intervening seven years since, six years since the summer of 1992, have you ever seen or heard or had any contact with Mohamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have never obtained any piece of information about him. He was seen the last time in Omarska. There are certain people who saw him there. But for the past seven years, we haven't received any information on him. The International Red Cross has him listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Who were some of the other SDA leaders in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, Dr. Rufus Suljanovic, Mr. Meho Terzic, Professor Ilijaz Music, Mrs. Valida Mahmuljin, Ilijaz Memic, Becir Medunjanin, Avdo Mujkanovic, Islam Bahonjic, Denija Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Of those people you that just mentioned, since the summer of 1992, how many of these people are you aware of that still survive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the people I mentioned, I know that three are alive. Out of twenty leaders of the municipal board, I know that three are alive, plus myself, four that is. Of course, I didn't give you an exhaustive list of these people, but if necessary, I could provide you with a complete list of these leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who were the leading members of the SDS in Prijedor municipality that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the SDS leaders were the following: Dr. Srdja Srdic, Mr. Dragan Savanovic, Simo Miskovic, Milomir Stakic, Dr. Milan Kovacevic, Mr. Dusan Kurnoga, Mr. Dragan Sidjak, Mr. Simo Drljaca, and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And other than Mr. Simo Drljaca, whose circumstances we're all aware of, to your knowledge, do all of those individuals -- or are all of those individuals still alive in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I have heard from some of them that they no longer live in the area of Prijedor, that they live in Cyprus. That is what I heard. But according to the information I have, I know that they are all alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Might that be a good time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn now, twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, after the initial government -- initial offices were assigned in the municipality of Prijedor, were there continuing problems in reaching agreement on candidates for other municipal positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the disagreements over? What were some of the positions that were in contention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Agreement was reached only concerning people at leading positions and their deputies. However, problems arose concerning the appointment of officials within the police and the public auditing service, or SDK as it is known in Serbo Croat, and in some other functions as well, but these two positions are the two that I remember best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the particular difficulties with those positions? Why were they so contentious?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were lots of difficulties because the SDA, as the winning party, had the right to appoint the Chief of Police and the Chief of the Public Auditing Service. However, the Serb Democratic Party did not agree with that, and they wanted to appoint the Chief of Police and the President or the chief of SDK. This was a major obstacle and a number of discussions were held, but no agreement could be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why was it important to the SDA to have the position of Chief of Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For SDA, it was very important because it was one of the pre-electoral promises to the voters. We promised them that if we win, we would finally have our Chief of Police because, for a number of years, for maybe 40 years, a Muslim was never appointed to the office of the chief of police, and according to the results of the census, the area was predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the SDA demand with respect to the Chief of Police -- sorry, SDS demand? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS demanded that they be given that office. They had their own candidate. I believe that they proposed Simo Miskovic to that post, who had already retired. However, regardless of their candidate, we wanted to stick to our electoral right and to make good the electoral promise to our voters, so we wanted to have -- we insisted on having that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How was the issue resolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The issue was resolved to our advantage, and Mr. Hasan Talundzic was elected to that post as the candidate of the Party of Democratic Action. He became Chief of Police. But, of course, it was only after very long and difficult negotiations and it was in consultations with our central party boards, SDA and SDS respectively, and in the end, the SDS had to accept the principles that had been agreed upon at the level of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you please describe the nature of the relationship between the central offices of the party at the republic level and the municipal offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For all important issues, central offices of the party were responsible, the offices in Sarajevo. Both SDS and SDA had their central offices in Sarajevo. They established criteria, they issued directives or orders concerning the implementation of political decisions that were made at the higher level. These criteria and these orders or directives had to be honoured because it was in this way that each party implemented their policies, policies that were agreed upon at the highest level and that were then implemented at the municipal level. So all municipal leaders or municipal committees would refer issues -- would refer, if there are any problems, to the central offices in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, you've described the nature of the relationship between the parties at the Opstina level. Can you describe, please, the nature of the relationship between the parties in the Republic Assembly of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was almost identical, the relationship was almost identical at the level of the Republic. Here I have in mind the relationship between the leadership of the parties, that is, between central offices of the parties. I am familiar with that situation because I was a member of the parliament. We had a number of sessions, they were very long, and during the breaks, representatives of each party would meet together and hold their internal meetings; and I had an opportunity to exchange views with members of the SDS, members who had certain instructions and directives from their central offices in relation to parliamentary issues, the adoption of laws and things like that. Everything that happened at the level of the Republic was then transferred to the level of the municipality. This was especially the case with the SDS. And when it comes to Prijedor, the SDS did not fully follow the directives from the SDS office in Sarajevo. Very often, they would block the implementation of certain things for which they had orders. The division of power was agreed upon at the level of the Republic, but they did not accept their proposals, and they posed a number of obstacles. In the end, they had to accept the proposals given by the Republic, but it was only upon the insistence of their central offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You have mentioned taking part in discussion with SDS officials in the republic assembly. Did any of those discussions regard the situation in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them, yes. I discussed the situation in Prijedor with Mr. Srdja Srdic most often, he was the president of the SDS in Prijedor, and he was the deputy to the Republic Assembly, Parliament. Sometimes we would travel together to parliament sessions, and we also had opportunity to talk during the breaks when we would wait for the next session to begin. Likewise, I had several opportunities to discuss these matters with Mr. Timarac, who was a deputy to the republic parliament. He was from Prijedor and he was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In any of your conversations with Srdja Srdic, would he engage in serious conversations about the problems in Prijedor with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he wouldn't. There was a need for us to talk because the situation was getting more complex. However, all my attempts to have a conversation with him would boil down to an exchange of anecdotes or jokes, and in the end, our conversations would be rather comical and we couldn't agree on anything in connection with the problems in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you a witness or part of conversations with SDS officials from outside of Prijedor where they discussed the issue of Prijedor with Srdja Srdic or the other members of the Prijedor delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, during the breaks, between sessions at the parliament. We had a room upstairs where we could have a cup of coffee during the break and where representatives from various parties would get together. Sometimes they would be separate, but I didn't pay much attention to that, and I often talked to all of them. Sometime in mid-1991, I had opportunity to listen to various critiques concerning the work of Srdja Srdic and the situation in Prijedor. I vividly remember one particular occasion where an SDS representative, Mr. Ljubo Bosilicic (phoen), who I believe was from Pale, where he attacked very fiercely Mr. Srdja Srdic, and a number of deputies joined him, and his main concern was that Srdja Srdic hadn't done anything in Prijedor, that he hadn't organised the Serb people in the municipality of Prijedor, he didn't know what Srdja Srdic was waiting for, why he wasn't doing anything, and so on. The essence of that conversation was a little strange to me. This was something that I couldn't understand. I had a very definite view of the electoral process. Elections had taken place, and I simply saw no point in some further organising of the people, and that is why the very essence of these criticisms eluded me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As these difficulties in establishing cooperation in the government continued, both at the Republic and municipal level, was there a movement by the SDS and other Serb politicians to separate from the democratically elected government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As early as August 1991, certain things started happening, things that were not fully in accordance; that is, they were not at all in accordance with the law and the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In July, in Herzegovina, some kind of autonomy was proclaimed, and on the 1st of August, in the territory of Banja Luka, certain events took place which were later on discussed at the level of the Republic, within the parliament. The TV relay at Kozara in Lisina was captured, and this all resulted in the change of the situation in the field and in the change of atmosphere in general from the psychological point of view, because the media, in this case the TV, had completely lost any connection with the republic, with the centre of the republic. So we raised that issue. We wanted to know why this was happening. The SDS stated publicly that they had nothing to do with that and that this issue should be discussed at some other level. At the local level, in Prijedor, members of the SDS told us that they didn't know who had done that and they didn't know the reason why this had been done and that this was something that they were opposing and that the police should do their own job, the police should resolve that problem. So we tried a number of official channels, but it was not possible to resolve that problem. It was not possible to have access to the TV transmitter. But this put us in a very difficult situation because we could no longer follow the programme of the Sarajevo television, and all broadcasts we could receive were from Serbia or the Belgrade TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, focusing on events in the summer and early fall of 1991 outside of the political events, what significant events were occurring in Slovenia and Croatia at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First in Slovenia and then in Croatia, the Yugoslav People's Army carried out a military intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As that conflict, particularly in Croatia, built up, was there a call for mobilisation by the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was a call for mobilisation issued by the JNA. The state leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not agree with that call for mobilisation, but it was issued anyway. In accordance with the existing legal provisions, the JNA could not mobilise people for the war against Croatia, people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the call-up papers were distributed, and the media conducted a mass campaign. They included the Serb television and the local Banja Luka TV station which was established in September in '91. They had a number of reports from the battlefield in Croatia. A campaign was conducted to that effect. At the beginning, it was under the pretext to protect Yugoslavia, and later on it became quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, after the mobilisation call was issued, what was the response from the elected government in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The elected government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was against the intervention of JNA in Slovenia and Croatia. In the meantime, these two states gained their independence, and with that act also the laws of Yugoslavia did not apply anymore. In the parliamentary discussions, I discussed and pointed out these matters, and they insisted on negotiations and insisted on the withdrawal of JNA from Croatia and that it stop military operations there. However, there was no success in this endeavour of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the SDA and HDZ parties support that position, both at the Republic level and in the Opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the level of the Republic, it was supported by SDA, HDZ, by The League of Communists, the other opposition parties, but SDS was for mobilisation and for the military operations in Croatia. So SDS held totally opposite position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was that also the same scenario in the Opstina of Prijedor itself, in the local Assembly, within the local politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely the same. And also in the local Assembly, quite similar debates were carried on. The Serb representatives were accusing the Bosniaks in the municipal assembly that they were supporting the Ustasha because they don't want to wage battles against them. They also stated that Prijedor has to be defended in Croatia and not in Prijedor itself, and therefore, we don't want to defend Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you say "we don't want to defend Prijedor," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs told us, "You don't want to defend Prijedor because you don't want to fight in Croatia because Prijedor is to be defended in Lipik and Pakrac and not in Prijedor itself."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Despite the position, the official position of the government, did some Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats volunteer for service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know some of those individuals who volunteered from the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew -- the number was symbolic of these volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After these individuals returned from Croatia, as an elected representative in a local community, did you go to speak to them about their experiences in Croatia and what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. I talked to them and I talked to a young man whom I knew quite well, Elezovic Salih, he was a lieutenant in the reserve, and when he received the call-up papers, he accepted them and he went to Croatia. He was there for some time and availed himself at the first opportunity to abandon and to desert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he describe to you the treatment of the Bosnian Muslims within the JNA during their service in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. First of all, he said that there were very few and that they were often derided. They were the object of jokes for a number of reasons: Firstly, because there were few of them there, because they didn't know some traditional Serb songs and cannot sing with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What kind of insults or comments, derogatory comments, were made toward them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually they labelled them as Turks. Turks. That was always as a joke but it was also always derogatory. They joked at their expense because they didn't eat pork.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And an ever-greater number of the soldiers weren't bearing the insignia of JNA. The insignia were diverse, with -- then some insignia from the Second World War. For example, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am going to interrupt you for a moment. Mr. Keegan, we're going somewhere away from Prijedor at the moment. Let's return there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At this time, as a result of this particular mobilisation, did there then result an uneven balance in the ethnic composition in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. In the JNA at that time, we had a predominant majority of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: (Note: Counsel states objection prior to interpretation being completed) ... we are too far afield from Prijedor. If he wants to testify about the composition of the JNA in Prijedor, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did this same disparity also exist in the Opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I wish to say to the Trial Chamber that we had a garrison with some 100 soldiers. During the period under discussion, thousands and thousands were mobilised, and in Prijedor, there was officially an entire brigade which was then transferred to the war theatre in Croatia, and that brigade, the composition of the brigade, was almost exclusively Serb, almost exclusively Serb soldiers. It was the 6th Krajiska brigade and later on the 5th Kozarska brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During this time, while this was going on, did the parties nevertheless continue to try and work with the SDS to prevent a further separation and continuing difficulties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, we tried -- we were attempting this on a daily basis and incessantly, but it was very difficult. On the level of the republic, there was an agreement between the parties; namely, to cooperate. But for us, it was very difficult to have any success in that because the Prijedor municipality was overcome by this war euphoria and a great percentage of the Serb population signed up for mobilisation. The brigade was formed, it was sent to Croatia, it returned to Prijedor, and when they were returning home for a few days' vacation, they didn't dispose of their and did not hand in their weapons and ammunition to the depots but sent it home. They would shoot in the air, and this was disturbing the local population. SDS had very good cooperation with the military, they had identical views concerning the issue of mobilisation, and it was very difficult for us to establish cooperation because we didn't believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time Defence moves the non-responsive part of the answer be stricken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. The record is being made, and we can't remove it. Motions to strike are not recognised here. Now, what is the objection? We'll get on more quickly if we don't have interruptions. What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is the difference because of the system where I practice, and I apologise because this is not the practice here, so -- I'm getting used to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document now being handed is labelled 5.9 on the exhibit list. It is a document agreed to by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You recognise this document, Mr. Semenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Yes, I recognise it. In the beginning of August, due to an ever-increasing number of incidents in the field, the Party of Democratic Action, together with the Serb Democratic Party and the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, succeeded in drafting an agreement in view of this situation, that they establish monitoring groups on the level of municipalities to monitor the situation and to calm the situation where necessary, and this was also signed by the president of the Serb Democratic Party, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and this document is, in fact, information to the municipal committees and an instruction that on the level of municipalities, the SDS appoints two members of joint monitoring committees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were these monitoring groups ever established? Was this agreement ever implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. On the municipal level, according to the -- in line with these instructions, no. No, we didn't succeed in that, although we attempted many times. We succeeded in that only in two or three local communes, but on the municipal level of Prijedor, there was never an attempt to create such a monitoring group and to make that piece of information public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated earlier that during the same period of time -- we're now talking the fall of 1991 -- that the SDS initiated, began moving away from the elected government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they, in fact, initiate the development of a separate political structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't receive any official information from the SDS that they're doing that, operating in that direction, but on the basis of their act and their work, we concluded that such a process is underway. In fact, we asked a number of times why the cooperation isn't more intense, why certain events are occurring, whether they are setting up their parallel system. The response was always negative, no way, and that they had nothing to do with the incidents which were occurring.
